newsitem.title: USA: U.S. 1996 trade deficit grows as December deficit widens.
newsitem.headline: U.S. 1996 trade deficit grows as December deficit widens.

text.p: Record imports drove the U.S. trade gap sharply higher in December and pushed the nation's shortfall on goods and services trade for 1996 to an eight-year peak, the Commerce Department said on Wednesday.

The deficit climbed 29.6 percent to $10.29 billion from a revised $7.94 billion in November, bringing the total 1996 trade gap to $114.23 billion -- an 8.7 percent jump from 1995 and the highest since a $115.5 billion shortfall in 1988.

Analysts warned that the dollar's rising value will swell the deficit further in 1997 by making U.S.-made products more costly in foreign markets. But Clinton administration officials vowed renewed efforts to broaden sales opportunities in booming Asia.

Soaring costs for imported oil pushed up both the December and full-year deficit figures, while lackluster economies in western Europe provided a less buoyant market for American products in December.
"I think we haven't seen the worst of it yet," said Lawrence Chimerine, chief economist for the Economic Strategy Institute in Washington.
"We haven't seen the full lagged impact of the dollar's rise but we're already seeing Japan taking a large share back of U.S. auto markets," he added.

Chimerine predicted the deficit will exceed $130 billion in 1997, especially if exchange rates continue to favour strong exporters like Japan and China, which together accounted for more than half of the United States' 1996 trade shortfall.
Commerce Secretary William Daley sought to put a positive spin on the figures. "Our competitiveness is unquestioned in the world," he told a news conference.
Daley pledged "an aggressive stand" in opening up Japan's and China's protected markets without specifying any details.
The shortfall between exports to China and imports from it climbed 17 percent in 1996 to $39.52 billion. That was second only to a $47.68 billion bilateral deficit with Japan.

The dollar's value climbed more than 8 percent against the German mark and almost 12 percent against the Japanese yen last year. It has continued to surge this year and economists note there is generally a lag between its appreciation and any measureable impact on trade.
The Commerce Department said the U.S. trade gap, excluding petroleum, actually declined last year for the first time in four years, to $107.79 billion from $111.72 billion in 1995.
The December deficit exceeded Wall Street economists' expectations of a $9.9 billion shortfall. Previously, the department said the November deficit was $8.4 billion, but it revised that downward.
Markets took the deteriorating trade picture in stride, with little evident impact on either bond or stock prices. The dollar dipped briefly but by midday was rising once more against Japan's yen.

"This number is nothing exciting. Combined with the downward revision to November's deficit, this data was about what the Commerce Department assumed in its fourth-quarter GDP report," said John Ryding, managing director and senior economist at Bear Stearns & Co. Inc.
Overall imports during December grew by 1.5 percent to a record $81.68 billion, while exports declined 1.6 percent to $71.4 billion.
Crude petroleum imports jumped 13.3 percent in value to $4.66 billion in December as the price per barrel increased to $21.65 from $21.44 in November.

Capital goods imports, including computers and telecommunications equipment, grew by $464 million in December to $19.55 billion. Imports of consumer goods also were up, possibly in part because of late stocking for the Christmas holiday season, by $525 million to $15.28 billion.
The politically sensitive deficit with Japan actually decreased in December by 1.2 percent to $4.27 billion while the gap with China was down 11.7 percent to $2.65 billion.
The trade deficit with Canada soared 32.8 percent to $2.32 billion in December while the gap with Western Europe shot up 48.7 percent to $2.05 billion.
In trade with oil-producing OPEC countries, the United States posted a December deficit of $1.89 billion, up 28.7 percent from $1.47 billion in November.
The United States typically runs a surplus on its trade with other countries in services like travel and tourism that partly offsets big merchandise trade deficits.
The merchandise deficit swelled 16.2 percent to $16.58 billion in December and hit a record $187.62 billion for all of 1996.
The surplus on services fell 0.7 percent to $6.29 billion in the month but for the full year was a record $73.39 billion.
In trade with Mexico, the United States had a $667 million deficit in December, down by 56 percent from the shortfall of $1.52 billion recorded in November.
